hook: Trying to reassure yourself that you're fine is one of the things most likely to keep your anxiety running. Here's why.
body:
**Trying to reassure yourself that you're fine is one of the things most likely to keep your anxiety running.**

When you tell yourself "it's fine, it's not a big deal, I'm being irrational" — your brain doesn't receive that as resolution. It receives it as continued engagement with the threat.

The act of reassurance signals that there is something to reassure yourself about. Your nervous system notes that you are still actively managing a perceived problem. It stays alert.

This is also why seeking reassurance from other people often doesn't work — or works for 20 minutes before you need another dose. You haven't resolved the signal. You've just suppressed it temporarily with external input.

The reassurance loop is one of the most counterintuitive patterns in anxiety because it feels like a solution. It produces immediate mild relief. But it keeps the system engaged with the threat rather than releasing it.

What works instead is acknowledgment without analysis. "I notice the signal is running. It doesn't require a response right now." Not arguing with the anxiety. Not investigating it. Letting the activation complete its cycle without feeding it more material.

The full guide on this — including the exact language — is in the free resource linked in my bio.
